title: Chewy Vendor Deductions Guide for Pet Brands: Sept 2026
summary: Pet brands absorb heavy Chewy deductions. Learn which shortage and compliance claims are invalid and how to win disputes. September 2026.
body_markdown:
Chewy is the largest online pet retailer in the U.S., with roughly[$12.6 billion in annual net sales](https://investor.chewy.com/news-and-events/news/news-details/2026/Chewy-Announces-Fiscal-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results/default.aspx) and 21.3 million active customers. More than 80% of what it sells goes out through recurring Autoship orders, which tells you everything about the cadence a supplier is dealing with: steady volume, but a relentless stream of invoices. And deductions compound faster for pet brands than almost any other CPG category. Most of the revenue lost to them is recoverable. High repurchase rates mean more deduction events and more disputes racing toward hard deadlines, so getting a handle on what Chewy actually deducts for, and why, is the first step to keeping revenue you've already earned.


**TLDR:**


- Chewy vendor deductions are automatic short-pays built into your vendor agreement, covering shortages, compliance chargebacks, price discrepancies, and marketing fees.
- 40 to 60% of shortage deductions across retail are invalid, tied to receiving errors rather than actual missing product, and a signed BOL is your primary dispute weapon.
- Compliance chargebacks stack on a single shipment: a missed appointment with no notice runs $1,000, ASN and fill-rate failures are charged at 5% of the cost of goods on the affected units, and pallet violations run $50–$100 each (per Chewy's Vendor Compliance Manual v4.6).
- Pet food brands absorb deduction volume harder than most CPG categories because high repurchase rates mean constant invoice volume and more deduction events to contest.
- Glimpse disputes and recovers invalid deductions for pet brands as a fully managed service, and brands see an average 2.5% revenue lift from recovery alone.


## What Are Chewy Vendor Deductions?


Chewy vendor deductions are amounts Chewy withholds directly from a vendor payment when a shipment, document, or compliance requirement falls short of its routing guide. If your invoice is $10,000 and Chewy's remittance comes in at $9,200, that $800 gap is a deduction.


These are B2B financial penalties between Chewy and its vendors, not consumer chargebacks or credit card disputes. The deductions are built into your vendor agreement and applied automatically, often before you know something went wrong.


By the time a short-pay hits your AR, Chewy has already made its call and moved on.


## The Most Common Deduction Types Pet Brands Face


Most Chewy deductions fall into four recurring buckets. Knowing which one you're looking at tells you whether you have a legitimate dispute or an internal process to fix — the sections below break each down in detail.


- **Shortage deductions:** Chewy claims it received fewer units than you invoiced.
- **Advertising and marketing deductions:** co-op fees, promotional allowances, and sponsored placement charges, some authorized and some not.
- **Compliance chargebacks:** penalties for routing-guide violations like labeling, late delivery, or fill-rate misses.
- **Price discrepancy deductions:** Chewy's PO price and your invoice price don't match.


## How Chewy's Vendor Model Creates Deductions


Chewy operates as a first-party retailer, which means when you sell to Chewy, you're selling to them directly. It buys your inventory, sets the retail price, and manages the customer relationship. That structure gives Chewy real pricing power over vendors, and it shows up in the deductions it takes.


The volume of these deductions scales with your revenue. A brand doing $2M annually on Chewy can absorb them manually. A brand doing $20M will see them pile up fast, and the window to recover closes whether or not your team is keeping up.


## The Main Types of Chewy Vendor Deductions


Chewy runs a deduction-heavy vendor program, and the charges fall into a few distinct buckets. Knowing which type you're dealing with shapes how you dispute it and whether you have a realistic shot at recovery.


### Shortage Deductions


These are the most common and the most contested. Chewy claims it received fewer units than invoiced and deducts the difference. Industry data puts the invalid rate for shortage deductions at 40 to 60% across retail, typically tied to receiving errors or mismatched documentation instead of product that was actually missing. Pet brands can find a deeper breakdown of how to recover these claims in the guide to[pet CPG invalid retail deductions](https://www.tryglimpse.com/post/pet-cpg-shortage-deductions-dispute) .


### Advertising and Marketing Deductions


Co-op fees, promotional allowances, and sponsored placement charges. Some are contractually agreed upon. Others get applied without clear authorization, and those unauthorized deductions are recoverable.


### Compliance Deductions


Chargebacks for labeling issues, late shipments, fill rate misses, or EDI errors. These carry strict dispute deadlines and often require backup documentation to contest effectively.


### Price Discrepancy Deductions


Chewy deducts when its purchase order price and your invoice price don't match. These can stem from outdated POs or internal pricing errors on either side.


## Chewy's Chargeback Schedule: What Each Violation Actually Costs


Chewy's Vendor Compliance Manual spells out its chargeback matrix, and the charges are material enough to plan around. One thing to get straight up front: not every chargeback is a flat fee. Several of the heaviest ones are assessed as 5% of the cost of goods on the affected units, and several are waived entirely if you stay above a monthly performance threshold. Chargebacks are accumulated across the month and applied as deductions in a later billing cycle, so you're disputing after the fact, not before.


Chargeback What triggers it Deduction


No Call No Show (NCNS) Missed delivery appointment with no advance notice $1,000 per missed appointment


Reschedules Appointment rescheduled inside 48 hours $750 per appointment (waived if monthly reschedule rate ≤ 4%)


ASN Fill Rate (ASNFR) Shipped short of the quantity on the ASN (EDI 856) 5% of COGS on units not received/overfilled (waived if within ±1% of 100%)


ASN On Time (ASNOT) ASN not transmitted at least 1 hour before delivery 5% of COGS on the affected units (waived if monthly ≥ 99%)


POA Fill Rate (POAFR) Shipped short of the quantity acknowledged on the POA (EDI 855) 5% of COGS (waived if monthly ≥ 95%)


PO On Time Delivered after the requested delivery/pickup date 5% of COGS on late units (waived if monthly ≥ 95%)


Pallet Damaged Pallet received damaged or non-compliant $50 per pallet


Pallet Refusals Pallet refused at receipt (unsafe or non-compliant) $100 per pallet


Value Added Service (VAS) Chewy re-labels or re-packs to make product compliant $100 per PO + per-unit application cost


Source: Chewy Vendor Compliance Manual v4.6 (February 2026), Vendor Chargeback Matrix.


A single shipment can hit several of these at once. A late truck with a missing ASN, a damaged pallet, and a fill-rate miss generates four separate charges against the same remittance: PO On Time (5% of COGS), ASN On Time (5% of COGS), Pallet Damaged ($50), and POA Fill Rate (5% of COGS). None of them require Chewy to notify you in advance. They're aggregated across the month and deducted in a later cycle.


Labeling is worth a specific callout, because it's often misunderstood as a flat per-carton fine. Label, carton, and marking noncompliance is chargeback-eligible, but the actual cost shows up as a Value Added Service charge ($100 per PO plus a per-unit cost) when Chewy has to re-label or re-pack to make your product compliant.


### Freight Accessorials and Rejection Charges


Separate from the compliance matrix, Chewy recoups transportation costs caused at the vendor's facility as off-credit deductions at the invoice level on collect full-truckload loads. These are easy to overlook and add up fast.


Charge Amount


Loading detention $100/hour after 2 free hours


Layover at shipper $250/day


Truck ordered not used $250/order


Re-work & redelivery $250/pallet (max $3,500/load)


Disposal $500/order


Product return Under 125 mi: $500 flat · Over 125 mi: $4/mile


## Why Pet Brands Feel Chewy Deductions Harder Than Other CPG Categories


Pet brands face a structural deduction problem that most CPG categories don't. Chewy's business runs on high-volume consumables, food, treats, and litter, where a single order can contain dozens of SKUs shipped to a fulfillment center under tight receiving windows. That operational complexity creates more opportunities for deductions to fire, and more of them to fire incorrectly. The same dynamics appear in[PetSmart vendor deductions](https://www.tryglimpse.com/post/petsmart-vendor-deductions-cpg-guide) and Petco vendor deductions, where high-SKU pet orders face the same tight receiving windows.


The category dynamics make it worse. Pet food has some of the highest repurchase rates in CPG, which means your invoice volume never lets up. More invoices means more deduction events. More deduction events means more disputes to manage. Most brands don't have the headcount to keep up, so valid disputes expire uncontested.


There's also a margin reality specific to pet. Public pet brand gross margins have a median of roughly 35%, per Eightx Pet Brand Financial Benchmarks 2026, compared to 50%+ in many beauty and supplement categories, so a 2% or 3% deduction rate hits differently. What might be a rounding error for a high-margin supplement brand is a meaningful chunk of operating income for a pet food brand running at that margin level, making it a direct driver of[CPG margin leakage](https://www.tryglimpse.com/post/stop-cpg-margin-leakage-improve-ebitda) .


The hidden costs of CPG chargebacks extend beyond the dollar amount deducted: they include the operational drain of managing disputes manually at scale.


## Shortage Deductions on Chewy: How They Work and Why They Stick


Chewy's shortage process works like this: it receives a shipment, counts the units, and files a claim if its count falls below your invoiced quantity. Critically, Chewy does not inspect merchandise on initial receipt. Signing for a shipment only means receipts will be reconciled after the receiving process, and Chewy notifies vendors of damages and shortages (except concealed ones) within 7 business days of receipt. For pet food brands, heavy items and multi-carton pallets see a higher rate of discrepancy claims because of how product moves in transit: weight shifts, cartons get miscounted, and receiving errors happen.


The documentation is what decides these disputes. A signed Bill of Lading from your carrier, matched against the corresponding invoice, gives you a concrete basis to push back. Without both documents aligned, the deduction holds regardless of what you actually shipped.


> "Shortage deductions aren't the easiest to win, but they are the most verifiable. There's a clear-cut paper trail." — Dexroy, deductions expert


Shortage deductions are the most documentable category in Chewy's deduction mix. Clean paperwork wins here more reliably than in almost any other deduction type, as Evermark's invalid shortage deductions recovery shows at scale.


## Spoilage and Expiration Claims on Pet Food


Shelf life is one place where Chewy's requirements are unusually explicit, and they cut against the vendor. Chewy guarantees its customers at least 90 days to expiration, and to back that it requires:


- Perishable products: a minimum of 180 days to expiration at time of receipt at any fulfillment center.
- Cold-chain products: a minimum of 90 days (refrigerated facilities: 105 days, or 15 weeks).
- Any product received short of those windows is disposed of at the vendor's expense, and disposal carries its own $500 charge plus potential re-work and return fees.


For EDI vendors, sending expiration dates on the ASN is mandatory for perishable shipments.


The practical takeaway is the opposite of "wait and dispute." Because the shelf-life test is applied at receipt, the way to protect this revenue is upstream: ship with comfortable runway against the 180-day (or 90/105-day cold-chain) standard, put accurate expiration dates on every ASN, and keep lot-level traceability so that if a disposal charge does post, you can show what shipped and when. Where a charge doesn't match your documented dating — a wrong lot referenced, or product that clearly met the window at receipt — that's your dispute, filed inside the 60-day chargeback window with the shipping records to back it.


## How to Dispute Chewy Vendor Deductions


Disputing Chewy deductions is a race against a fixed clock. Chargeback disputes must be submitted within 60 calendar days of the monthly chargeback notification. Miss that window and the deduction is permanent. Everything goes through the Chewy Partner Hub (cph.chewy.com/home); disputes sent by email or phone don't count. Chewy reviews and returns a decision within about five business days.


Here is a step-by-step breakdown of what an effective dispute process looks like:


1. Pull open chargebacks from the Chewy Partner Hub, sorted by notification date oldest to newest. Those hit the 60-day wall first.
2. Match each one to its backup: signed BOL, proof of delivery (a BOL stamped and signed by an authorized Chewy FC representative), invoice, and PO.
3. Cross-reference each deduction against your internal records to classify it as valid or invalid before writing a single dispute.
4. File through the Partner Hub with the chargeback type, dollar amount, and the specific documentation that refutes the claim. Submit each chargeback type separately per vendor number.
5. Track every open dispute by status and deadline. For metrics with waiver thresholds (fill rate, on-time, reschedules), file only after the monthly notification posts a charge.


Two more deadlines shape recovery. Proof of delivery for unpaid-invoice and shortage inquiries must reach Chewy within 90 days of the invoice due date, and Chewy won't investigate anything older than six months. And because Chewy reconciles after receiving rather than inspecting on the dock, a signed BOL matched to the invoice is the tool that wins shortage claims.


The real problem most brands run into is bandwidth. Running this process across hundreds of deductions per month, while managing other retailer relationships, is where valid disputes get dropped. Deductions that go uncontested are written off permanently once the dispute window closes.


Unmanaged deductions stack up fast across a multi-retailer portfolio. That's not a process problem you fix by hiring more people. It's a scale problem you solve with a fully managed service.

## The Documentation Stack That Wins Chewy Deduction Disputes


Each Chewy deduction dispute lives or dies on the backup you attach. Without the right documents, even a legitimate dispute gets denied, and you're left writing off revenue that was never actually owed.


Here's what a winning documentation stack looks like:


- The original purchase order and invoice, matched line by line to what Chewy received and what they're now claiming as a shortage or pricing discrepancy.
- Your proof of delivery, including carrier confirmation and pallet counts, which directly counters shortage deductions where the claim doesn't align with what was actually shipped.
- Any promotional agreements or deal sheets that confirm the pricing Chewy was charged, covering you against unauthorized deduction claims tied to pricing disputes.
- Screenshots or exports from Chewy's Partner Hub showing the chargeback notification date, which you'll need to confirm you're still inside the 60-day dispute window before filing anything.


One thing brands consistently miss: Chewy's dispute portal requires documents in specific formats, and submissions with the wrong file type or incomplete attachments get rejected. That rejection does not reset your dispute clock.

## FAQ


### What are the most common Chewy vendor deductions pet brands should know about?


The most common Chewy vendor deductions are shortage claims, compliance chargebacks, price discrepancy deductions, and co-op or marketing fees. Shortage deductions are the highest-volume category and also the most frequently invalid, typically resolving in your favor when you have a signed Bill of Lading and matching proof of delivery. Compliance chargebacks cover fill-rate and on-time failures, missed appointments, labeling issues, and EDI errors, and they carry a hard 60-day dispute window in Chewy's vendor program.


### How do I dispute shortage deductions on Chewy?


Pull the signed Bill of Lading from your carrier, match it against the corresponding invoice, and submit both through the Chewy Partner Hub with a clear reference to the deduction type and dollar amount. Chewy's portal rejects submissions with wrong file formats or missing attachments, and that rejection does not reset your dispute clock, so get the documentation right before you file.


### What documentation do I need to win a Chewy vendor deduction dispute?


A winning dispute package for Chewy deductions requires the original purchase order and invoice matched line by line, your proof of delivery with carrier confirmation and pallet counts, any promotional agreements covering the pricing period, and a record from the Chewy Partner Hub confirming you're still inside the 60-day dispute window. Missing even one document gives Chewy grounds to deny the claim outright, regardless of whether the underlying deduction is valid.


### Why do CPG brands write off so many retailer deductions instead of disputing them?


CPG brands write off deductions primarily because dispute windows are short, documentation is scattered across multiple portals, and the per-deduction effort isn't worth it for small-dollar claims when managed manually. A small compliance chargeback might take 45 minutes to document and file. At scale, that math doesn't work.


Brands doing meaningful volume across several retailers face hundreds of deductions per month, and internal AR teams simply don't have the bandwidth to contest everything before deadlines expire. The result is that valid disputes go unfiled, and those write-offs compound into substantial annual revenue loss that gets absorbed as an operating cost and never recovered.


### How does deduction management work for brands selling into Walmart or Target?


Deduction management at Walmart runs through their APDP (Accounts Payable Dispute Portal), where vendors file disputes with backup documentation (BOLs, invoices, and proof of delivery) against specific deduction codes. Target uses a similar vendor portal model with its own compliance chargeback structure. In both cases, the dispute process requires matching each deduction to the right documentation, submitting in the correct format, and tracking open cases against hard deadlines. Glimpse manages this process across Walmart, Target, and every other retailer in a brand's portfolio as a fully managed service, so brands aren't running separate workflows for each retail partner.


### Chewy vendor deductions vs. Walmart or KeHE deductions: is the dispute process meaningfully different?


Chewy's dispute process runs entirely through its Partner Hub on a 60-day chargeback window, more portal-specific than Walmart's APDP workflow and less EDI-dependent than KeHE's SPS Commerce setup, but the core documentation requirements overlap: BOLs, PODs, and invoice matching drive recovery across all three. The biggest difference with Chewy is that compliance chargebacks, co-op fees, and shortage deductions can stack against a single shipment in ways that add up fast, especially for high-SKU pet food orders with tight receiving windows.


### How do I recover cash from invalid chargebacks that retailers take off my invoices?


Recovering cash from invalid retail chargebacks requires three things: identifying which deductions are actually invalid, assembling the right backup documentation (signed BOL, invoice, proof of delivery, and any promotional agreements), and submitting a formal dispute through the retailer's vendor portal before the dispute window closes. For shortage claims, a signed Bill of Lading matched to the invoice is the primary recovery tool. For compliance chargebacks, you need to show the shipment met the routing guide requirements at the time of delivery. Once a dispute window expires, the deduction becomes permanent. There is no appeal after the deadline. Brands running this manually across multiple retailers miss a large share of recoverable claims due to bandwidth constraints, which is the core problem a fully managed service like Glimpse solves.

Dispute everything you can document, regardless of dollar size. Pet brands with high invoice volume see small deductions add up to large annual write-offs, and Chewy's dispute windows close permanently once they expire.
